kurz: How losses from capital assets are offset in two separate pots, which deadline applies in December and when a loss leads to a tax refund.

bloecke.md:
A realised loss in the portfolio is not automatically offset for tax purposes; it can only be used under strict rules. Section 20(6) sentence 1 EStG (Income Tax Act) rules out offsetting losses from capital assets against other types of income. They reduce neither wages nor rental income nor income from a business, and loss carryback under Section 10d EStG is expressly excluded. The only option is to carry the loss forward within the same type of income. This carryforward is unlimited in time, but it can only be used where positive capital income arises later.

Many people underestimate the fact that a portfolio loss in a year without capital income initially brings no tax benefit. It is carried forward and only used in the year in which it is matched by a suitable gain. That may also be ten years later.

Losses from capital assets can only be offset against capital income, never against wages or rent. Carrying them back to earlier years is ruled out; carrying them forward to later years is unlimited in time (Section 20(6) sentences 1 to 3 EStG).

Within capital income, there is a further restriction. Under Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG, losses from the sale of shares may only be offset against gains from the sale of shares. All other items, that is, fund units, bonds, certificates, derivative transactions (Termingeschäfte), interest and dividends, go into a second, general pot. The banks reflect this technically and keep, for each customer across all of their securities accounts, a share loss pot (Aktienverlusttopf) and a general [[Loss offset pot (Verlustverrechnungstopf)|loss offset pot (Verlustverrechnungstopf)]].

The restriction only works in one direction. A loss from the general pot may be offset against any positive capital income, expressly including gains on shares. A share loss, by contrast, may only be offset within its own pot. All the special cases that follow in this lesson can be derived from this asymmetry.

bloecke.titel: How realised losses can be offset
bloecke.unter: Legal position in 2026. The lower path leads to all income, the upper one only to gains from share sales.

bloecke.md:
The share loss pot is narrower than its name suggests. It only covers the sale of shares within the meaning of Section 20(2) sentence 1 no. 1 EStG. It does not cover:

- Units in funds and ETFs, including pure equity ETFs. They are taxed as investment income under the Investment Tax Act (InvStG) and therefore belong in the general pot.
- Dividends, because a dividend is not a capital gain. Investors who sell individual shares at a loss and also receive dividends cannot offset the two against each other.
- Certificates, warrants and bonds, even if they relate to shares.

For fund investors, this has one advantage and one disadvantage. A loss on an equity ETF can be used universally and may also be offset against interest and dividends. On the other hand, the [[Partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)|partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)]] works symmetrically. For an equity fund, 30% of the income is tax-free (Section 20 InvStG), and likewise 30% of a loss is disregarded for tax purposes. A book loss of €3,000 thus becomes an offsettable loss of €2,100.

“My share losses offset the gains in my portfolio.” This is only true for gains from share sales. A typical portfolio consists of an ETF savings plan and a few individual shares that have performed poorly. It generates share losses for which there are no matching gains, because ETF gains, dividends and interest do not count. The losses are carried forward year after year and remain unused until another share is eventually sold at a gain.

As long as all securities are held at one bank, the bank handles the offsetting automatically and on an ongoing basis. Each new item of income is first offset against the matching pot, and only the remainder is taxed (Section 43a(3) sentence 2 EStG). The bank automatically refunds capital income withholding tax (Kapitalertragsteuer) already withheld during the course of the year. With two banks, this automatic process no longer applies, because each institution only knows its own securities account. The following model case shows what this costs.

bloecke.titel: Model case 2026 with one investor and two banks

bloecke.md:
The calculation uses 26.375% (capital income withholding tax plus solidarity surcharge, without church tax). The [[Exemption order (Freistellungsauftrag)|exemption order (Freistellungsauftrag)]] has already been used up elsewhere.

At Bank A, the share pot comes to 4,000 − 7,000 = −€3,000, an excess that remains unoffset. The general pot contains €2,000 of positive income, against which the share loss may not be offset. The tax is €527.50.

At Bank B, the ETF loss of €2,100 is deducted from the share gain of €5,000. This is allowed because the ETF loss sits in the general pot. That leaves €2,900, and the tax is €764.87, because fractions of a cent are disregarded for the solidarity surcharge.

In total, €1,292.37 is withheld. At Bank A, a share loss pot of €3,000 remains and is carried forward to 2027, even though €5,000 of share gains were taxed at Bank B in the same year.

Combining the two is possible, but it must be actively requested and is subject to a deadline. Under Section 43a(3) sentence 4 EStG, the bank issues a [[Loss certificate (Verlustbescheinigung)|loss certificate (Verlustbescheinigung)]] for the loss not offset, on request. Under sentence 5, the request must reach the bank by 15 December of the current year, and it is irrevocable. Once the certificate is issued, the bank no longer carries the loss forward internally. The pot is reset to zero, and the loss is claimed through the tax return.

This procedure is mandatory. Under Section 20(6) sentence 5 EStG, losses that were subject to capital income withholding tax may only be offset if such a certificate has been issued. Without it, the tax office may not offset the losses at one bank against the gains at the other, even if the tax certificates have been filled in completely.

Share pot across both banks: 4,000 − 7,000 + 5,000 = +€2,000. General pot: 1,200 + 800 − 2,100 = −€100. This remainder may be offset against the remaining share gains, because this direction is allowed.

The taxable amount is €1,900, and the tax is €501.12. Since €1,292.37 was withheld, €791.25 is refunded. The share loss pot is thus completely used up, and nothing is carried forward.

bloecke.titel: Four items in one assessment (model case 2026)
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation. This route requires a loss certificate and only works because the general loss may also be offset against share gains. In the opposite direction, offsetting would be ruled out.

schritte.titel: Check the position at the beginning of December
schritte.text: Look at both loss pots of every securities account. Most banks show them in online banking under “Taxes” or in the interim income statement for the year to date.
Check whether gains matching the respective pot were taxed at another bank in the same year. Share losses only match share gains; all other losses match all income, including share gains.

Request the loss certificate in writing; the request must reach the bank by 15 December. Without matching gains in the same year, the bank-internal carryforward is the simpler solution, unless accumulated losses are to be formally assessed by the tax office.

Collect all tax certificates and report every securities account in the [[Capital income annex (Anlage KAP)|capital income annex (Anlage KAP)]]. Reporting only some of them is not enough, because the tax office only offsets what it has in front of it.
Any remaining loss is assessed separately. The notice shows share losses and other losses separately. These amounts form the balance for the following years.

bloecke.md: The request cannot be withdrawn, and the pot at the bank is empty afterwards. If the certificate is requested and no tax return is then filed, the loss is recorded neither at the bank nor at the tax office. The certificate alone achieves nothing; only the tax return leads to a loss carryforward. The request is therefore only worthwhile together with a tax return. It makes sense if offsettable gains arose at another bank in the same year or if losses accumulated over years are to be formally assessed by the tax office.

## Bank-internal and tax loss carryforward

The bank-internal loss pot is a technical account at the bank concerned. It is carried forward automatically, but it is tied to that institution. If the account is closed or only some of the securities are transferred, the pot does not go with them. Only if all assets are transferred in full to another securities account must the transferring institution notify the new bank of the outstanding loss, and only if the customer requests this. No certificate is issued in this case (Section 43a(3) sentence 6 EStG).

The loss carryforward for tax purposes, by contrast, only arises through the tax return. The tax office assesses it separately under Section 20(6) sentence 3 in conjunction with Section 10d(4) EStG, split into share losses and other losses. This balance is preserved through every change of bank, every closure of a securities account and even the insolvency of a broker. Investors who have accumulated larger losses over the years are therefore better off having them assessed once by the tax office, rather than leaving them with a single bank.

## Current rules for derivative transactions and worthless securities

Two special rules that were much discussed for years no longer apply. From 2020 and 2021 respectively, losses from the default of capital receivables and from derivative transactions could only be offset up to a limit of, most recently, €20,000 a year (Section 20(6) sentences 5 and 6 EStG, former version). As a result, active traders could in some circumstances have to pay tax even though they had made an economic loss. A trader who gained €300,000 and lost €320,000 paid tax on €280,000. In its order of 7 June 2024 (VIII B 113/23), the Federal Fiscal Court (BFH) expressed serious constitutional doubts about this restriction. The Annual Tax Act 2024 (Jahressteuergesetz) of 2 December 2024 deleted both sentences without replacement, with effect for all open cases.

Today, losses from derivative transactions and from the default or worthless expiry of securities and receivables go into the general pot without any limit on the amount. The exception is shares that have become worthless: under the circular of the Federal Ministry of Finance (BMF) of 14 May 2025 (para. 118), their losses count as share losses and may only be offset against share gains. Losses that a bank still recorded as default losses under the old law until it changed over its systems go into the general pot for the sake of simplicity. The banks must apply this allocation in tax deduction from 1 January 2026 at the latest, so tax certificates for 2025 may still differ depending on the institution. Guides and forum posts that calculate with €20,000 are out of date.

bloecke.titel: Loss offsetting since the introduction of the flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)
bloecke.unter: The share loss pot has existed unchanged since 2009; the offsetting limits for derivative transactions and defaults only applied for around four years.

ereignisse.titel: Introduction of the flat-rate withholding tax
ereignisse.text: It brings the share loss pot under Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG, which still applies today.
Losses can now only be offset up to, most recently, €20,000 a year; for defaults on receivables, this already applies from 2020.
In its order of 7 June 2024 (VIII B 113/23), the BFH expresses serious constitutional doubts about the offsetting limit.
The act of 2 December 2024 abolishes both restrictions without replacement, in all open cases.
Losses from shares that have become worthless count towards the share loss pot. Only losses already recorded under the old law go into the general pot for simplicity (para. 118).
The institutions apply the rule in tax deduction from 1 January 2026.

bloecke.titel: The share loss pot before the Federal Constitutional Court
bloecke.md:
The Federal Fiscal Court considers the unequal treatment of share losses compared with all other capital losses to be objectively unjustified. It has therefore referred Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG to the Federal Constitutional Court (BVerfG) by order of 17 November 2020 (VIII R 11/18; pending there under 2 BvL 3/21). Until a decision is made, the provision remains applicable, and in September 2026 it stands unchanged in the statute.

The main practical consequence is that share losses carried forward should be assessed through the tax return, so that they are available if the law changes. Whether and when the Federal Constitutional Court will decide, and whether new rules would apply retroactively, is open. An investment or sale decision should therefore not be made dependent on the outcome of these proceedings.

In addition to the two loss pots, the bank keeps a pot for creditable foreign [[Withholding tax|withholding tax]]. Unlike the loss pots, it is not carried forward; it lapses at the end of the year. The withholding tax is credited against the flat-rate withholding tax that remains after the year's losses have been offset. If the losses cancel out all of the year's income, the credit is lost, because without German tax there is nothing against which the withholding tax could be credited. This is another reason why losses should not be realised indiscriminately in the last days of December.

- The loss pots should be checked in December, not only in March. After 15 December, a loss certificate is no longer possible for the current year.
- Loss offsetting takes priority over the exemption order. Anyone who realises many losses does not use up their saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag), and the unused amount lapses because it is not carried forward.
- For spouses assessed jointly who have a joint exemption order, the bank offsets across the securities accounts of both spouses (Section 43a(3) sentence 2 EStG). In many cases, this replaces the certificate.
- Realising losses deliberately is only worthwhile if the position is to be sold anyway. The spread, the order fee and a possible re-entry at a higher price can quickly outweigh the tax advantage. After a repurchase, [[FIFO]] applies again to later sales from the holding.

mitnehmen: Capital losses can neither be offset against other types of income nor carried back; the only option is an unlimited carryforward within capital income.
The restriction only works in one direction: general losses may also be offset against share gains, but share losses only against share gains.
Losses from funds and ETFs count towards the general pot, but they are reduced by the partial exemption by 30%, 15%, 60% or 80%.

There is no automatic offsetting across several banks; this requires a loss certificate, which must be requested irrevocably by 15 December and is worthwhile if there are matching gains at another bank in the same year or if accumulated losses are to be assessed by the tax office.

The €20,000 offsetting limits for derivative transactions and defaults on receivables were abolished without replacement by the Annual Tax Act 2024, and calculations that still take them into account are based on outdated sources.

begriffe.text: Bank-internal account for losses from the sale of individual shares. Under Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG, these losses may only be offset against gains from share sales, not against dividends, interest or fund gains.

Bank-internal account for all other losses from capital assets, that is, from funds and ETFs, bonds, certificates, derivative transactions and defaults on receivables. These losses may be offset against any positive capital income, including share gains.

Separate assessment of the remaining loss carryforward by the tax office under Section 20(6) sentence 3 in conjunction with Section 10d(4) EStG, split into share losses and other losses. It only arises through the tax return and, unlike the bank-internal pot, is independent of the bank.
Bank-internal memo item for creditable foreign withholding tax. Unlike the loss pots, it is not carried forward and lapses at the end of the year.
